Which hygiene habits in your kitchen could be improved?
What does the story in Daniel 1 teach, and what does it not teach, about food?

blocks.text: A full stomach is not always a well-fed body; aim for variety, cleanliness and care.

sections.title: 5. Give children food they like to eat

blocks.text: 5. Give children food they like to eat.
And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
Why liking matters

The last point of the leaflet is very practical: food only nourishes a child if the child actually eats it. A parent may prepare the most nutritious meal, but if the child refuses it day after day, it does little good. Giving children food they like to eat is not spoiling them. It recognises that children are persons with real tastes and preferences, and that a happy eater is more likely to be a well-fed child.

Luke 2:52 records that the boy Jesus “increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.” Growth in stature – the growth of the body – is named alongside wisdom and favour. Caring for a child’s body, including their enjoyment of food, is part of caring for the whole child.
Balancing liking with nourishment

This point must be read together with the fourth. Children should be given food they like, but not only the foods they like. If left entirely to choose, many children would eat sweets, biscuits and soft drinks all day. A helpful balance is this: parents decide which healthy foods are offered and when meals take place, and children are allowed some say in how much they eat of what is offered. This respects the child without handing over the whole menu.
Offer new foods many times

Children are often cautious about new foods. A child who refuses a vegetable today may accept it next week or next month; children often need to be offered a new food many times before they accept it. So do not give up after one refusal, and do not quickly decide, “My child does not eat beans.” Offer a small amount again on another day, without pressure. Let the child touch it, smell it or taste a tiny bit. Over time, familiarity often turns refusal into acceptance.
Include a familiar food

When you introduce something new, place it beside at least one familiar food the child already likes. A child who sees their favourite fried plantain on the plate will come to the table happily, and may be willing to try the unfamiliar vegetable beside it. In this way each plate can hold something the child enjoys and something that helps them grow.
Involve children in food

Children are more willing to eat food they have helped to choose or prepare. Take older children to the market and let them choose between two vegetables or two fruits. Let them help with safe tasks suited to their age, such as washing vegetables, picking stones out of beans, stirring a cold mixture or setting the table. Keep young children well away from fire, hot oil, boiling water and sharp knives. Talking about where food comes from, and thanking God for it together, also helps children value what they eat.
Parents show the way

Children copy what they see. If parents refuse vegetables, drink soft drinks at every meal or complain about food, children are likely to do the same. When children see their parents enjoying fruit, vegetables and water, and giving thanks for simple meals, they learn that these things are normal and good. Eating together as a family, as the marriage leaflet encourages, is one of the best ways to model healthy eating.
Do not use food as a bribe or a punishment

Ephesians 6:4 tells fathers not to provoke their children to wrath, but to bring them up in the nurture and admonition – the loving training and instruction – of the Lord. Mealtimes can easily become a battlefield that provokes anger and fear. Avoid forcing children to clear the plate, threatening them, or pushing food into their mouths. Avoid using sweets as a reward for eating vegetables, which teaches children that vegetables are a punishment and sweets are the prize. Above all, never withhold food from a child as a punishment. Food is a gift from God and a basic need, not a tool of discipline.
When to see a health worker

Some children are simply choosy eaters, and this often improves with patience. But certain signs should never be ignored. Take your child to a clinic, primary health centre, doctor or other qualified health worker if your child shows any of these signs:

items: Losing weight, or looking thinner than before.
Falling sick often.
Swollen feet.
Not growing well, or falling behind in growth.
Refusing food and drink for a long time, or seeming unusually weak or tired.

blocks.text: Many clinics check children’s growth by weighing and measuring them regularly. Make use of these services, and seek help early rather than waiting until a child is very ill.
Practical steps

items: Ask each child to name two or three healthy foods they enjoy, and build some of the week’s meals around them.
Put one familiar food your child likes on every plate, beside anything new.
When a food is refused, offer a small amount again on another day, without pressure or comment.
Let older children choose between two vegetables or two fruits at the market, and give them a safe kitchen task suited to their age.
Eat the same healthy foods yourself, and let your children see you enjoying them.
Stop using sweets as a reward for eating, and never withhold a meal as a punishment.
Take young children for regular growth checks at the clinic, and seek help early if any of the warning signs above appear.

blocks.text: A family prayer over meals

Taken together, the two leaflets point to one picture: a family gathered around the table, thankful to God and caring for one another. You may use this prayer, or your own words, before a family meal:

*Heavenly Father, thank you for this food and for the hands that prepared it. Thank you for our home and for each person at this table. Bless this meal to our bodies, and help us to love one another in word and in deed. Provide for those who have no food today, and make us generous to share. In the name of Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.*
Questions for reflection

items: Which foods do your children most enjoy, and how can you combine them with foods that help them grow?
How do you usually respond when a child refuses a new food? What might you do differently?
In what ways could your children help with choosing or preparing food?
Why is it important never to use food as a bribe or a punishment?
Looking back over the whole booklet, what one change will you make to show love more clearly in your home?

blocks.text: Offer good food with patience and love, and your children will learn to receive it with thanks.
